title: To Cross, or Not to Cross Pages for Prefetching?
problem: L1D cache prefetchers operating with virtual addresses can issue prefetch requests across page boundaries, but whether page-cross prefetching is beneficial or harmful is workload- and phase-dependent, and existing prefetchers lack the intelligence to selectively enable or suppress these cross-page requests.
method: MOKA is a holistic framework for designing Page-Cross Filters that attach to existing L1D prefetchers. It combines three components: (i) hashed perceptron predictors using prefetcher-independent program features (PC, stride, memory access history) to estimate page-cross benefit, (ii) system-state-adaptive predictors that account for TLB pressure and MSHR occupancy, and (iii) a dynamic phase-switching scheme that periodically recalibrates filter decisions across changing execution phases. The resulting prototype filter, DRIPPER, is instantiated for Berti, IPCP, and BOP prefetchers without modifying their core logic.

title: Mixed-Precision Quantization for Deep Vision Models with Integer Quadratic Programming
problem: Uniform bit-width quantization causes significant accuracy degradation at low precision and inefficiency at high precision; existing mixed-precision methods assume independence of layer quantization errors, leading to suboptimal assignments.
method: CLADO approximates pairwise cross-layer quantization errors using linear equations learned on a small data subset, then assigns layer-wise bit-widths via Integer Quadratic Programming that explicitly models these dependencies to optimize the accuracy-efficiency frontier.

title: SQ-DM: Accelerating Diffusion Models with Aggressive Quantization and Temporal Sparsity
problem: Diffusion models require many inference steps for high-quality generation, limiting practical deployment; aggressive quantization and sparsity are difficult to exploit due to time-variant sparsity patterns that vary across channels and timesteps.
method: SQ-DM applies 4-bit aggressive weight and activation quantization combined with channel-specific activation sparsity that evolves per timestep; a custom accelerator with heterogeneous mixed-precision dense-sparse architecture, channel-last mapping, and timestep-aware sparsity detection handles the dynamic patterns efficiently.

title: 19.11 A 13GHz Charge-Pump PLL Achieving 15.8fsrms Integrated Jitter and -98.5dBc Reference Spur
problem: Modern RF-sampling communication systems (wideband data converters, complex modulation) impose stringent phase-locked loop (PLL) requirements: ultra-low jitter and near-zero reference spurs. Sub-sampling PLLs achieve superior low-frequency phase noise but suffer large reference spurs from BFSK effects. Sampling PLLs avoid periodic VCO modulation but are limited by available loop gain (K_stope). Charge-pump PLLs dominate industry but their in-band phase noise, set by charge-pump characteristics, makes ultra-low jitter challenging.
method: A dual-path charge-pump PLL architecture integrating: (1) Resistive-discharge time-amplifying phase-frequency detector (RD-TAPFD) improving charge-pump linearity, (2) Series-resonance VCO (SR-VCO) with over-voltage protection suppressing phase noise, (3) Sampling-based filter achieving sharp low-pass response without large capacitors. The dual-path design balances in-band phase noise suppression via increased phase-detector gain while maintaining robust lock acquisition.

title: 2.5 A 16nm 5.7TOPS CNN Processor Supporting Bi-Directional FPN for Small-Object Detection on High-Resolution Videos
problem: Small-object detection in high-resolution (2M-pixel) images requires deep networks (77-layer backbones) with multi-scale feature extraction, but high memory bandwidth and compute requirements limit deployment in energy-constrained and mobile scenarios.
method: 16nm CNN processor combining orientation-interleaved-causally-processed (OICP) modeling for bi-FPN feature-map memory reduction, bandwidth-optimized backbone scheduling (RARC re-access/re-compute), and reconfigurable tensor engine (RTE) supporting diverse operations, achieving 5.7TOPS throughput.

title: A Hardware-Software Design Framework for SpMV Acceleration with Flexible Access Pattern Portfolio
problem: Sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV) is difficult to accelerate due to highly irregular data access patterns that vary by input matrix structure. Static accelerators optimized at compile time cannot handle the dynamic matrix structures encountered in large practical SpMV workloads.
method: SPASM is a hardware-software co-design framework that extracts local data access patterns from input matrices and derives a portfolio of template patterns to encode matrix tiles. A reconfigurable hardware computing structure supports vectorized computation and flexible run-time switching between different template patterns per tile. Global composition analysis of input matrices drives hardware configuration and workload scheduling to improve load balancing across parallel processing units. The template portfolio can be optimized for expected input sets while retaining flexibility for unseen patterns.

title: CogSys: Efficient and Scalable Neurosymbolic Cognition System via Algorithm-Hardware Co-Design
problem: Neurosymbolic AI workloads—combining neural network inference with symbolic reasoning (e.g., probabilistic logic, abduction)—exhibit high memory intensity, compute heterogeneity, and irregular access patterns that cause severe underutilization on commodity CPU/GPU/TPU hardware.
method: CogSys is an algorithm-hardware co-design framework with three layers: (1) Algorithm: an efficient tensor factorization technique to reduce the compute and memory footprint of symbolic reasoning operations; (2) Hardware: a scalable ASIC architecture with reconfigurable neuro/symbolic processing elements (nsPEs) and a bubble streaming (BS) dataflow with spatial-temporal (ST) mapping that enables highly parallel, pipelined execution of heterogeneous neural and symbolic kernels; (3) System: an adaptive workload-aware scheduler (adSCH) that orchestrates the assignment of neural vs. symbolic kernels to nsPEs for high resource utilization, evaluated under TSMC 28nm.

title: Pirate: No Compromise Low-Bandwidth VR Streaming for Edge Devices
problem: High-quality VR streaming for edge devices requires simultaneously satisfying two competing demands: extremely low bandwidth (the edge uplink is constrained) and real-time rendering at high frame rates (90 FPS), while previous approaches sacrifice one for the other.
method: Pirate exploits stereo similarity—the high structural redundancy between left-eye and right-eye VR video frames—to avoid transmitting both views. Only one eye's view is transmitted at any time, alternating left and right, together with precomputed disparity maps and optical flow information. The target eye view is iteratively synthesized on-device from the single transmitted view using only this lightweight geometric information (no large ML model), at extremely low bitrates down to 0.1 bits per pixel. The alternating transmission schedule further amortizes bandwidth by recycling synthesized frames across time.

title: AQB8: Energy-Efficient Ray Tracing Accelerator through Multi-Level Quantization
problem: Ray tracing BVH traversal is bottlenecked by DRAM bandwidth consumed by 32-bit floating-point bounding boxes, and prior 8-bit compression schemes still require decompression back to FP32 for intersection tests, retaining the arithmetic cost of complex FP32 operations.
method: AQB8 constructs a quantized BVH tree using a multi-level quantization scheme where bounding boxes are encoded as 8-bit integers at multiple hierarchy levels, enabling intersection tests to operate directly on low-bit integers without decompression. The hardware replaces FP32 arithmetic units with area-efficient integer units for BVH traversal, eliminating both DRAM bandwidth waste and expensive FP32 arithmetic. A hierarchical error-compensation mechanism propagates quantization bounds across BVH levels to prevent false-negative ray-box misses.

title: Uni-Render: A Unified Accelerator for Real-Time Rendering Across Diverse Neural Renderers
problem: Existing neural rendering accelerators are designed for a single specific rendering pipeline, making them unable to efficiently support the diverse and evolving landscape of neural rendering algorithms (NeRF, 3DGS, hybrid methods) required for different application scenarios.
method: Uni-Render is a reconfigurable hardware ASIC accelerator that identifies common operators shared across diverse neural rendering pipelines (ray marching, Gaussian rasterization, MLP inference, volume compositing) and implements a configurable dataflow engine that dynamically adjusts dataflow and operator mapping to match the computational profile of each specific rendering algorithm. The hardware architecture supports both typical and hybrid rendering pipelines through runtime reconfiguration of its processing elements and memory hierarchy.

title: G-SpNN: GPU-Accelerated Passivity Enforcement for S-Parameter Modeling with Neural Networks
problem: Passivity enforcement in high-frequency circuit macromodeling encounters convergence issues and accuracy compromises; the Domain-Alternated Optimization (DAO) framework requires additional optimization but suffers from high memory consumption and slow convergence for large-scale problems.
method: G-SpNN recasts passivity-enforced macromodeling as a neural network training problem, leveraging GPU acceleration to significantly enhance convergence speed and memory efficiency. The approach translates domain constraints into neural network regularization objectives.

title: GSAcc: Accelerate 3D Gaussian Splatting via Depth Speculation and Gaussian-centric Rasterization
problem: GPU-based 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering suffers from insufficient parallelism in sequential pipeline stages and large memory overhead for intermediate results.
method: GSAcc introduces Gaussian depth speculation to parallelize preprocessing and sorting. A Gaussian-centric dataflow interleaves preprocessing and rasterization, executing all steps concurrently without storing intermediates. Dedicated hardware accelerates sorting and rasterization.

title: Towards Uncertainty-aware Robotic Perception via Mixed-signal BNN Engine Leveraging Probabilistic Quantum Tunneling
problem: Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) provide uncertainty quantification essential for safety-critical robotic perception, but traditional software BNNs have prohibitively high hardware overhead and latency, restricting real-time deployment on resource-constrained robots.
method: Mixed-signal hardware accelerator leverages probabilistic quantum tunneling in fully depleted silicon-on-insulator (FDSOI) transistors to generate Gaussian random variables efficiently (200 fJ/sample, r=0.997 correlation). Parallel BNN architecture uses this compact randomness source for low-latency probabilistic inference.

title: FABRIC8LABS Electrochemical Additive Manufacturing ECAM Enabled Thermal Solutions for the Al Data Center
problem: Data center cooling consumes significant power and space; traditional liquid and air cooling systems scale poorly as chip power density increases.
method: ECAM (Electrochemical Additive Manufacturing) enables precise 3D manufacturing of custom copper cooling structures. These structures provide direct chip-to-liquid cooling with optimized heat transfer paths and minimal pressure drop.

title: Local-GS: An Order-Independent Gaussian Splatting Training Accelerator Exploiting Splat Locality
problem: 3D Gaussian Splatting training on edge devices is bottlenecked by depth-wise data dependencies between overlapping Gaussians, limited memory, and hardware under-utilization. Order-dependent rendering requires sequential processing, preventing parallelism exploitation.
method: Local-GS introduces order-independent rendering to break depth-wise dependencies, enabling parallel pixel intersection test unit scheduling based on Gaussian splat locality. Unified training-rendering cores execute efficient splat-level parallel rendering and gradient propagation simultaneously, optimizing hardware utilization.

title: Unified Memory Protection with Multi-granular MAC and Integrity Tree for Heterogeneous Processors
problem: Hardware memory protection in heterogeneous SoCs (CPU + GPU + NPU) causes significant performance degradation because conventional fixed-granularity MACs and integrity trees are optimized for CPU access patterns but perform poorly under the diverse, irregular memory access patterns of GPUs and NPUs.
method: The authors propose a unified multi-granular MAC and integrity tree mechanism that supports four granularity levels for both MACs and counters. A multi-granular tree stores coarse-grained and fine-grained counters at different tree levels, and a dynamic detection mechanism selects the most appropriate granularity per memory region based on the observed access pattern from each processing unit. The design is further combined with prior sub-tree techniques to reduce tree traversal overhead.
